text:
From HTTPS Address to First Byte: What the Browser Does

When you type https://www.example.com/products into a browser and press Enter, a surprising amount of work happens before a single byte of the response arrives. Most of it takes milliseconds, but each step can fail or add latency, so knowing the sequence helps you debug slow pages and understand what tools like the browser's Network tab are showing you.

1. Parsing the URL and checking local state

The browser first splits the address into parts: the scheme (https), the host (www.example.com), the port (implicitly 443 for HTTPS), the path (/products), and any query string or fragment. The fragment (#section) is never sent to the server.

Before touching the network, the browser consults several local sources. The HSTS list tells it whether a host must only be reached over HTTPS, which lets it upgrade a typed http:// address without a network round trip. The HTTP cache may already hold a fresh copy of the resource, in which case the request can finish without any network activity at all. Service workers, if registered for this origin, may intercept the request and answer it themselves. Only if none of these satisfy the request does the browser go to the network.

2. DNS resolution

Networks route by IP address, not by name, so the browser must turn www.example.com into an address such as 203.0.113.10 (IPv4) or a 2001:db8:: style address (IPv6). It checks, in order, its own DNS cache, the operating system's cache and hosts file, and then asks a configured recursive resolver, usually run by your ISP, your company, or a public provider. If the resolver does not have the answer cached, it walks the hierarchy: it asks a root server which servers handle .com, asks those which servers are authoritative for example.com, and asks the authoritative server for the record. The answer comes back with a TTL (time to live) that controls how long each layer may cache it.

A cold lookup can take tens to hundreds of milliseconds; a cached one is nearly instant. Modern browsers may also query for HTTPS and SVCB records, which can advertise that the server supports HTTP/3 or provide other connection hints. If a site has several addresses, the browser typically tries them in a staggered fashion (often called Happy Eyeballs), preferring IPv6 but falling back to IPv4 quickly if the first attempt stalls.

3. Opening a TCP connection (or QUIC)

With an IP address, the browser needs a transport connection. For HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 this is TCP, established with a three-way handshake: the client sends SYN, the server replies SYN-ACK, and the client sends ACK. That costs one full round trip before any application data can flow. If the distance to the server means a 50 ms round trip, the handshake alone costs 50 ms, which is why content delivery networks put servers physically close to users.

HTTP/3 instead runs over QUIC, which uses UDP and folds the transport and encryption handshakes together, saving round trips. Browsers usually learn about HTTP/3 support from a previous response header (Alt-Svc) or a DNS record, so a first visit often still uses TCP.

Browsers also reuse existing connections. If a connection to the same origin is already open, for example from a previous page, steps 2 and 3 are skipped entirely. HTTP/2 can even reuse one connection for several hostnames if the certificate covers them and they resolve to the same address.

4. The TLS handshake

Because the scheme is https, the connection must be encrypted and the server authenticated before any HTTP is sent. This is TLS. With TLS 1.3, which most modern servers support, the handshake takes one round trip.

The client sends a ClientHello listing the TLS versions and cipher suites it supports, a random value, a key share for key exchange, and the Server Name Indication (SNI) extension carrying the hostname. SNI matters because one IP address may host many sites, and the server needs to know which certificate to present. The client may also list supported application protocols (ALPN), such as h2 and http/1.1, so protocol negotiation happens within the same handshake.

The server replies with its chosen cipher suite, its own key share, and its certificate chain. At this point both sides can compute the same shared secret using ephemeral Diffie-Hellman, and everything after the ServerHello is already encrypted. The server proves it owns the certificate's private key by signing the handshake transcript.

5. Validating the certificate

The browser verifies the certificate chain before trusting the server. It checks that the leaf certificate is valid for the requested hostname (via the Subject Alternative Name field), that it has not expired, and that it chains up through intermediate certificates to a root certificate authority already trusted by the browser or operating system. Revocation status may be checked through mechanisms such as stapled OCSP responses or the browser's built-in revocation lists. Browsers may also check that the certificate appears in Certificate Transparency logs. If any check fails, the browser stops and shows a full-page warning rather than sending your request. This is the step that stops someone on the same network from impersonating the site.

Once the client sends its Finished message, the secure channel is established. If you have visited recently, TLS session resumption can shorten this further, and TLS 1.3 even allows sending early data on a resumed connection, though that carries replay risks and is used cautiously.

6. Sending the HTTP request

Now the browser finally sends the request, encrypted inside the TLS session. In HTTP/1.1 it looks like text:

GET /products HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Accept: text/html
Accept-Encoding: gzip, br
Cookie: session=abc123

In HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 the same information is sent in a compressed binary format, but the meaning is identical: a method, a path, and headers. The browser attaches cookies that match the host and path, any cached validators (If-None-Match, If-Modified-Since) if it holds a stale copy, and headers describing its language and compression support.

7. Waiting for the server

The request travels to the server, often first reaching a CDN or load balancer that terminates TLS, then forwards it to an application server. That server routes the request, may query a database or call other services, and builds a response. This waiting period is what browser tools report as Time to First Byte (TTFB), though note that tools often include DNS, connection, and TLS time in that number. When the first bytes of the response, the status line and headers, travel back and reach the browser, the journey this description covers is complete.

Why this matters

Adding up the pieces for a cold visit: one DNS lookup, one round trip for TCP, one for TLS 1.3, and one for the request and response. That is roughly four round trips before content arrives, and every optimization you hear about targets one of them: DNS caching and prefetching, connection reuse, CDNs placing servers closer to users, HTTP/3, TLS resumption, preconnect hints, and fast server-side rendering or caching. When a page is slow, the Network tab's timing breakdown (DNS Lookup, Initial Connection, SSL, Waiting) shows you which stage is responsible, so you can fix the right one.
